items.headline: Israel holds 9,265 Palestinians as "security" inmates, a third of them without trial
items.dek: HaMoked's October figures from the Israel Prison Service show 3,101 administrative detainees and 1,419 people held as "unlawful combatants".
body: HaMoked's monthly count, based on data the Israel Prison Service provides, put the number of Palestinians held as "security" inmates at 9,265 at the start of October 2026: 1,509 sentenced prisoners, 3,236 remand detainees, 3,101 administrative detainees and 1,419 people held under the Unlawful Combatants Law.
Administrative detention, imprisonment on secret evidence with no charge, is down from a 2025 peak of 3,629 in July 2025 but remains more than double the 1,264 recorded in September 2023.
The sentenced population fell sharply during 2025, from 2,364 in September 2023 to about 1,500 now, so people held without a conviction now make up the large majority of the total.

items.headline: Ben-Gvir films himself telling a life prisoner he wants him executed
items.dek: The national security minister posted footage from inside the cell of Hassan Salama, drawing condemnation from Palestinian detainee bodies.
body: Israel's National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, who oversees the prison service, published a video on X showing him inside the cell of Hassan Salama, a Hamas figure serving multiple life sentences for 1996 bombings, and telling him he wanted him killed and executed.

The PA's Commission of Detainees and Ex-Detainees Affairs condemned the footage, and the Palestinian Prisoners Media Office called it an election stunt ahead of the 27 October vote, holding Israel responsible for Salama's safety.

Ben-Gvir said the clip was filmed about two weeks before it was posted. He used it to repeat his call for executing Palestinian prisoners, months after the Knesset passed the Death Penalty for Terrorists Law.

sources.title: Palestinians denounce Israeli minister Ben-Gvir's threats against prisoner

items.headline: Former detainees describe what happens off camera when the minister visits
items.dek: Ben-Gvir's own videos boast about harsh conditions; released prisoners say the beatings happen before and after filming.
body: Ben-Gvir has spent weeks broadcasting prison visits as achievements, including an AI-made clip of men entering a facility healthy and leaving emaciated, which he later deleted, and footage of himself telling a female prisoner the good conditions were over.

Photojournalist Muath Amarneh, from Dheisheh camp near Bethlehem, told Al Jazeera that the filmed moments are a fraction of the humiliation detainees experience around such visits. He has twice been held in administrative detention since October 2023.
Within a day of the report, the Palestinian Prisoner's Society said Amarneh had been arrested again.

sources.title: Inside Israel's prisons, where Ben-Gvir's cruelty is policy

items.headline: More than 100 West Bank arrests in a single week, children and journalists among them
items.dek: The Palestinian Prisoner's Society counted over 100 detentions in seven days, including a man freed in a prisoner exchange.
body: The Palestinian Prisoner's Society said Israeli forces detained more than 100 Palestinians across the West Bank in one week, describing field interrogations, beatings, threats to relatives and homes taken over for military use.
Those held included Ahmad al-Sayfi of Birzeit, released under a recent exchange deal, and journalists Muath Amarneh and Sabri Jibril.
The group puts West Bank detentions since October 2023 at more than 25,000, with thousands more taken from Gaza.

items.headline: Administrative detainee gives birth by C-section, then is returned to prison
items.dek: Dana Joudeh, 35, from Nablus, learned she was pregnant in custody; she was held without charge.
body: Dana Joudeh, a 35-year-old from Nablus held in administrative detention, gave birth by caesarean section at Rambam Hospital on 12 September and was taken back to prison two days later, The Intercept reported. She was due to be released on 15 September.
She had been held at Sharon Prison and then Damon Prison. Her daughter, Lia, was later moved to hospitals in Ramallah for neonatal care.
The Israel Prison Service rejected her account as false and said detainees receive the care they are entitled to, without discussing her medical details.

items.headline: Gaza hospital director nears two years in custody with no charge
items.dek: Six members of the US Congress called for Dr Hussam Abu Safiya's release as his lawyer reported continued beatings.
body: Dr Hussam Abu Safiya, director of Kamal Adwan Hospital, has been held since Israeli forces took him from the hospital on 27 December 2024. He has never been charged or tried.

In early September, Physicians for Human Rights Israel relayed testimony from his lawyer Nasser Odeh, who visited him in the Rakefet facility at Nitzan Prison and reported beatings with batons, sleep deprivation and threats.

On 6 October six Democratic members of Congress, including Rashida Tlaib and Ilhan Omar, issued a statement urging his release and citing at least 16 Palestinian physicians still in Israeli detention.

items.dek: Protesters at the World Medical Association assembly demanded the suspension of the Israeli Medical Association.
body: Health workers protesting outside the World Medical Association summit in Rotterdam hung 81 sets of scrubs, each labelled with the name of a Palestinian health worker held in Israeli detention.
The IMA Out! coalition accused the Israeli Medical Association of silence over the destruction of Gaza's health system and called for its suspension from the WMA.

items.headline: Supreme Court restores Arab lists to the ballot but pushes Balad's leader out
items.dek: Justices overturned the election committee's bans on Ra'am and the Joint List; Sami Abu Shehadeh withdrew under pressure.
body: The Central Elections Committee had voted to bar Ra'am and the Joint List, as well as MK Ofer Cassif and Balad chair Sami Abu Shehadeh, from the 27 October election.

On 2 October a nine-justice panel unanimously reinstated both lists and, by 7 to 2, reinstated Cassif. During the hearing the previous day, Supreme Court President Isaac Amit said a majority would uphold Abu Shehadeh's disqualification and suggested he withdraw, which he did.

Adalah, which represented the parties, said the case against Abu Shehadeh rested mainly on an analytical article he published on 8 October 2023, and that he is the first Palestinian leader pushed out of a Knesset race since the 1985 disqualification law.

items.headline: Court sends nine of ten settler suspects home within days of their arrest
items.dek: The men were held over attacks on a Washington Post photographer and European diplomats; one remains in custody.
body: Police arrested ten Israeli citizens on 19 October over the attack on harvesters and photojournalist Heidi Levine in Khirbet Abu Falah and the assault on French, Belgian and Polish diplomats near At Tayba.
A court in Jerusalem released nine of them to house arrest late on 21 October, according to the settlers' law firm Honenu; police said one suspect stayed in custody and the investigation continues.
Yesh Din's head of research Yonatan Kanonich said that in most attacks on Palestinians nobody is arrested at all, and that arrests tend to follow only when a case attracts media attention.

items.headline: High Court closes test case on telling families where Gaza detainees are held
items.dek: After two years, the court deleted HaMoked's consolidated petitions without the State ever stating its legal position.
body: HaMoked asked the High Court to rule whether, and how, the State must disclose the whereabouts of people held under the Unlawful Combatants Law. The court consolidated three habeas petitions about Gazans arrested in July 2024 and repeatedly let the State delay its answer.

On 21 August 2026 the State asked for deletion, saying the individual cases were resolved and that a separate 3 June 2026 judgment ordering it to resume cooperation with the ICRC covered the wider issue. The court deleted the petitions; HaMoked said the question of principle was left open.

Between October 2023 and October 2026 HaMoked filed 5,991 tracing requests for Gaza residents; in 2,015 of them the army answered that it had "no indication" of the person. Of 114 habeas petitions, 38 people were never located.

items.headline: Court lets a deported prisoner's wife leave the West Bank after reviewing the secret file
items.dek: HaMoked said it was the first time such a blanket travel ban on a relative was lifted in this way.
body: A West Bank woman whose husband was freed in a prisoner exchange and deported to Egypt was twice stopped at the Allenby crossing. The army's reply to her request said only that she was the wife of a deported "terrorist operative".

HaMoked filed an administrative petition on 11 May 2026 arguing that authorities must give reasons, as COGAT's own procedures require. After the court examined the security material, she was allowed to travel to join her husband.
HaMoked says the military denies thousands of travel requests a year on undisclosed security grounds, often aimed at relatives of released prisoners.

items.headline: Cabinet asks the army's top lawyer whether the new death penalty can be used
items.dek: After a deadly shooting at a spring, Ben-Gvir demanded the suspect be the first person sentenced under the March 2026 law.
body: An Israeli man, Netanel Chkroun, was shot dead on 20 September at a spring near Neveh Tzuf; the suspect was caught by an undercover army unit. Ben-Gvir said the attacker belonged on the gallows and raised the case in a security meeting.
Netanyahu asked military officials whether the Death Penalty for Terrorists Law could apply, and the security cabinet arranged a follow-up session with the Military Advocate General.

PCATI called it the first case in which the law could be used. In military courts the law makes death the near-default sentence for West Bank Palestinians convicted of deadly attacks; no charge had been reported when the coverage was published.

items.headline: Rights groups ask the Supreme Court to strike down the Death Penalty Law
items.dek: The Knesset passed the law 62-48 on 30 March 2026; the petition is still awaiting a ruling.
body: Hours after the Knesset passed the Death Penalty for Terrorists Law, Adalah, PCATI, HaMoked, Physicians for Human Rights Israel and Gisha, with MKs Aida Touma-Sliman, Ayman Odeh and Ahmad Tibi, filed an urgent petition (HCJ 76304-03-26).

The petitioners say the law is built to apply to Palestinians only: in West Bank military courts it makes death the near-mandatory sentence, allows a simple majority to impose it even when prosecutors do not ask, removes the commander's power to commute and requires execution within 90 days.
The court ordered the State to respond by 24 May 2026. No ruling on the merits had been reported by October 2026.

items.headline: Knesset creates a special military tribunal for October 7 suspects, with death sentences possible
items.dek: The law passed 93-0; Adalah says it strips defendants of basic fair-trial guarantees.
body: On 11 May 2026 the Knesset passed, 93 to 0, a law establishing a special military tribunal to try Palestinians held over the 7 October 2023 attack and the holding of hostages.
The tribunal may impose the death penalty, which Israel has not carried out since 1962. Adalah argues the procedure is incompatible with the presumption of innocence and judicial independence.

items.headline: First use of citizenship-stripping law reaches the Supreme Court
items.dek: The State wants to revoke the citizenship of a man who committed his offences at 17; Adalah asks the court to void the law.
body: In February 2026 Netanyahu filed the first motions under a 2023 amendment allowing revocation of citizenship for Palestinian citizens convicted of terror offences who received PA payments, followed by deportation to the West Bank or Gaza.

One target, Mohammad Ahmad al-Halaseh, was 17 at the time of his offences and is serving 18 years. After the Jerusalem District Court said the case raised constitutional questions, Adalah petitioned the Supreme Court on 30 April 2026 (HCJ 76360-04-26). It is pending.

items.headline: Masked settlers burn olive trees and beat a Washington Post photographer at Abu Falah
items.dek: About 80 settlers attacked harvesters; OCHA counted nine Palestinians and a foreign journalist injured.
body: Around 80 masked settlers descended on a terraced olive grove at Abu Falah, setting trees alight and throwing stones, some with slings. Soldiers who arrived fired tear gas towards Palestinians, according to Reuters reporting carried by LBC.

Veteran photojournalist Heidi Levine, 64, working for The Washington Post, was knocked down and kicked and needed surgery on a finger. Settlers also burned three cars in nearby Turmus Ayya that morning.
OCHA recorded nine Palestinians injured at Abu Falah, including a child, plus the foreign journalist. Police arrested ten suspects three days later.

items.headline: Harvest season already the worst on record for settler attacks
items.dek: OCHA logged 272 harvest-related attacks between 1 September and 19 October, more than any full season since at least 2024.
body: OCHA documented 272 settler attacks linked to the olive harvest from 1 September to 19 October 2026, killing one Palestinian and injuring 200. The totals already exceed the entire 2024 season (224) and 2025 season (185).
Ramallah governorate accounts for 164 of the attacks and Nablus for 52. On 7 October a 44-year-old man was killed in an attack on harvesters near Burqa and Bizzariya.
Military orders now require "prior coordination" for about 88,300 dunums of farmland, roughly 30 per cent more than last year, and more than 2,150 settler attacks have been recorded since January.

items.headline: At Tur demolition displaces 69 people, the largest single East Jerusalem displacement on record
items.dek: A five-storey residential building was razed; 36 of those displaced are children.
body: Israeli authorities demolished a five-storey residential building in At Tur on 6 October, displacing 69 Palestinians including 36 children. OCHA says it is the biggest displacement from one demolition in East Jerusalem since its records began in 2009.
A week later, on 13 October, three refugee households (16 people, 10 of them children) in At Tur lost their home when the owners demolished part of the building and the authorities razed the rest.
By 19 October about 1,790 Palestinians had been displaced by permit-related demolitions across the West Bank in 2026, 668 of them in East Jerusalem.

items.headline: Army razes every home in Khirbet al-Tabban
items.dek: Twelve homes and most other structures were destroyed after the High Court rejected the residents' petitions in June.
body: Israeli forces demolished all 12 homes in the Masafer Yatta hamlet of al-Tabban on 2 September, along with water tanks, animal pens and other structures. PCHR counted 38 structures and 58 people left homeless, 26 of them children.
PCHR says the buildings dated from 2002 to 2015, building permits and a local plan were refused, and the residents' High Court petitions were rejected in June 2026.
Nidal Younis, head of the Masafer Yatta council, said residents would stay and rebuild.

items.headline: Two Bedouin and herding communities demolished on the same day
items.dek: In Jinba 55 people were displaced and moved into caves; in Az Za'ayyem 33 lost their homes.
body: On 23 September demolitions in Jinba, inside "Firing Zone 918", displaced eight families (55 people, 32 of them children), who stayed on the land sheltering in caves.

The same day, 20 structures in the Bedouin community of Az Za'ayyem near Jerusalem were destroyed, displacing six households. Since 2009 more than 560 structures have been demolished in 18 Bedouin and herding communities around Jerusalem.
OCHA says about 400 structures have been demolished in Masafer Yatta over 15 years, displacing 969 people, and nearly half of those demolitions have happened since January 2025.

items.headline: Settlers torch homes as a displaced family tries to return under a court decision
items.dek: More than 100 settlers rioted in Jalud; the army then ordered the Tubasi family out again.
body: The Tubasi family had been displaced from Jalud for nearly two months and tried to go home under an Israeli court decision. Settlers set fire to two of their houses and to vehicles overnight on 28-29 September.
The army said more than 100 settlers rioted and blocked its attempt to facilitate the return. Local sources told Anadolu that soldiers then made the family leave again at gunpoint.
OCHA listed the incident as one of 53 settler attacks recorded in the West Bank that week.

items.headline: More than 3,000 Palestinians forced out of their homes in locked-down Hebron
items.dek: After two soldiers were killed, the army sealed the city, evacuated neighbourhoods and turned homes into posts.
body: Since a shooting on 23 October that killed two Israeli soldiers near Hebron, the army has sealed the city and ordered evacuations by loudspeaker at night. Defence Minister Israel Katz said residents would not return until the army had finished its work.

Hebron's governor put the displaced at 488 families, 3,171 people, across the governorate; the mayor said 3,043 are from the city itself. The Palestinian Prisoner's Society reported at least 71 arrests in four days.
Netanyahu and Katz said they would apply the "Jenin camp model", the approach used in 2025's Iron Wall operation in northern camps that displaced more than 33,000 people.

items.dek: More than 20 organisations condemned mass home demolitions in Arab Bedouin communities across the Naqab.
body: Adalah and more than 20 other civil society groups issued a joint statement on 19 October condemning mass demolitions of homes in Arab Bedouin communities in the Naqab, and warned of more ahead of the elections.
They asked governments to press Israel to halt the demolitions and provide adequate housing. The statement did not give a total number of homes destroyed.

items.headline: Khan al-Ahmar faces its demolition order again, with far less attention than in 2018
items.dek: Smotrich revived the orders in May 2026 to clear the way for the E1 settlement project.
body: The Jahalin Bedouin village of about 200 people lost its Supreme Court case in May 2018, but demolition was frozen that October after international pressure.
In May 2026 Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich revived the orders. The Nation reports that protests this time have been much smaller, and residents fear they can no longer hold off the bulldozers.
Of about 20 Bedouin villages in the E1 corridor between Jerusalem and Ma'ale Adumim, 18 would be destroyed under the plan.

items.headline: More than 1,500 killed in Gaza since the October 2025 ceasefire
items.dek: OCHA's weekly report records continued strikes, falling food aid and an unfunded winter.
body: Gaza's Ministry of Health has recorded 1,522 people killed and 5,421 injured since the ceasefire agreement, OCHA reported on 22 October, including 32 killed in the week to 19 October.

Food assistance reached 1.3 million people in September, down from 2.1 million in January, and is expected to fall below one million. About 60 per cent of the $283 million needed for winter shelter is unfunded.
Since the ceasefire 3,423 patients have been evacuated for treatment abroad, out of more than 13,800 since October 2023.

items.headline: Israel keeps moving the Yellow Line, now controlling about 65% of Gaza
items.dek: Families in Shujayea are moving their tents again as the concrete markers advance.
body: Under the October 2025 ceasefire Israeli forces withdrew behind the so-called Yellow Line. The UN says they now control about 65 per cent of Gaza, up from the 53 per cent agreed a year ago.
On 11 October the yellow blocks were moved several metres west in Shujayea. Mahmoud Harzeen, 35, told Al Jazeera he was preparing to move his family's tent for the sixth time.
The UN human rights office verified 331 deaths near the line between the ceasefire and the end of July 2026.

items.headline: WFP cuts food aid to half a million people in Gaza
items.dek: Funding for 2026 is less than half of previous years; rations are being halved.
body: The World Food Programme said it would reduce monthly assistance in Gaza from 1.6 million to 1.1 million people, cut rations from two food parcels per family to one, and cut hot meals from 250,000 to 150,000 a day.
WFP said it needs another $450 million to keep critical operations running in the occupied territory for six months.

items.headline: Israel confirms a Gaza detainee's death nearly two years after it happened
items.dek: Ihab Diab, 36, was arrested in December 2023; Palestinian officials believe he died in September 2024.
body: The Israel Prison Service told the Palestinian Commission of Detainees and Ex-Detainees Affairs that Ihab Mohammed Abdel Qader Diab, 36, from Gaza, had died in custody. He was detained on 12 December 2023; the commission believes he died around 18 September 2024.
Israel cited an underlying illness; his family says he was healthy when arrested and alleges torture.
The commission says 328 Palestinians have died in Israeli custody since 1967, 91 of them since 7 October 2023, including 53 from Gaza.

items.headline: Three years on, Gaza's recorded death toll passes 74,000
items.dek: The Ministry of Health counts only registered deaths; thousands remain under rubble or missing.
body: By the third anniversary of the war, Gaza's Ministry of Health had recorded at least 74,000 Palestinians killed, including at least 21,000 children, and more than 175,000 wounded.
By 26 October the ministry's count stood at 74,555, including 1,559 killed since the ceasefire took effect in October 2025.

items.dek: Rep. Rashida Tlaib backed the request, citing US obligations under the Genocide and Geneva Conventions.
body: The Hind Rajab Foundation filed an emergency request for the US Department of Justice to arrest Sean Glass, who it says commanded the unit implicated in the killing of five-year-old Hind Rajab, her relatives and the paramedics sent to reach her.
Tlaib said the US, as a party to the Genocide Convention and Geneva Conventions, is obliged to arrest and investigate him. No US response was reported.

items.headline: More than 2,000 Palestinian children detained since October 2023
items.dek: At least 350 are in Israeli prisons now; the Palestinian Prisoner's Society documents illness and starvation inside.
body: The Palestinian Prisoner's Society said Israeli forces have detained more than 2,000 Palestinian children since October 2023 and at least 350 are currently held. Six children from Hebron were arrested on 13 October alone.

It cited Mohammed Hamid, 15, who caught scabies in Ofer Prison, developed severe infections and later lost a leg, and Walid Ahmad, 17, who died in March 2025 after six months in Megiddo. A judge halted the inquiry into Walid's death in December despite evidence of starvation.
Two US citizens are among those held: Abdalkareem Safi, moved to an adult section at Ofer after turning 18 in detention, and Adam Karakrah, 16, whose bail release was reversed in August.

items.dek: Mohammed Zalbani was 13 when he was arrested; he is serving 18 years and his family is barred from visiting.
body: Mohammed Zalbani of Shu'fat camp was arrested in February 2023, aged 13, over a stabbing at a checkpoint; the soldier who was stabbed was then accidentally shot by a security guard and died. Mohammed was later sentenced to 18 years.
His mother Fidaa says she has not been allowed to visit Megiddo Prison for about two years. A lawyer told the family that child detainees there go to sleep hungry most days.

items.dek: New first- and seventh-grade classes in municipal schools must use only the Israeli curriculum.
body: The school year opened with an open-ended strike at private and Christian schools in East Jerusalem after Israel blocked entry permits for West Bank teachers and required all new first- and seventh-grade municipal classes to use the Israeli curriculum.
More than 45,000 Palestinian students, about one in three in East Jerusalem, are now in the Israeli programme, nearly four times the figure six years ago.

items.dek: Finn Joughin says he was seized by armed settlers after stepping in when settler teenagers tried to take over the pitch.
body: Finn Joughin, 22, a volunteer with Proactive Presence in Umm al-Khair, says settler teenagers and parents surrounded the village pitch on 29 August and he was abducted at gunpoint after intervening to protect Palestinian children.
Israel then deported him to Britain. Umm al-Khair, in Area C beside the Carmel settlement, has faced repeated settler attacks and demolition notices.

items.headline: The main Palestinian children's rights group shuts down
items.dek: Defense for Children International-Palestine stopped work on 7 April 2026; its last count found 351 children held, half without charge.
body: DCIP ended operations on 7 April 2026, citing Israel's criminalisation of Palestinian rights groups. Israel outlawed it as a "terrorist organization" in 2021 on largely secret evidence, and raided and sealed its Ramallah office in 2022; European states later found the accusations baseless.

Weeks before closing, DCIP reported that 51 per cent of the 351 Palestinian children in Israel Prison Service custody at the end of 2025 were in administrative detention, the highest number and share since it began tracking in 2008. Children in military interrogation centres are not counted.

items.headline: UN inquiry finds crimes against humanity in the West Bank and continuing genocide in Gaza
items.dek: The commission cites extermination, torture, rape and persecution; Israel called for the body to be dissolved.
body: The UN Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory said Israeli forces and settlers had committed crimes against humanity in the West Bank, including extermination, torture, rape and persecution, covering October 2023 to September 2026.
It recorded 254 Palestinians killed in air strikes in the West Bank since 7 October 2023, against six from 2008 to October 2023, and said genocidal acts in Gaza have continued despite the ceasefire.
Israel's mission in Geneva called the report misinformation and demanded the commission's dissolution. The report came out the day before Israel's general election.

items.headline: UK, France, Canada and nine others move to restrict trade with settlements
items.dek: Britain announced a ban on settlement goods; Israel responded by ordering the UK's Jerusalem consulate closed.
body: Foreign ministers of Canada, Denmark, Finland, France, Iceland, Ireland, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Spain, Sweden and the UK said they would introduce or support restrictions on trade in goods from settlements, which are illegal under international law.
The UK announced an import ban on settlement products. Israel retaliated by moving to close Britain's consulate in occupied East Jerusalem.

items.headline: UN adds 61 companies to its settlement business database
items.dek: The list now names 214 firms in 11 countries; five were removed.
body: The UN human rights office added 61 companies to its database of businesses involved in activities linked to settlements in the West Bank and East Jerusalem, bringing the total to 214 in 11 countries.

Most are Israeli, with others based in China, France, Germany, Luxembourg, Mexico, the Netherlands, South Africa, Spain, the US and the UK. A company is listed for at least one of ten activities, including building settlements, supplying surveillance equipment and providing banking.

items.headline: US sanctions the ICC itself; allies and the UN rally to the court
items.dek: The measures bar most transactions with the court after a six-month grace period.
body: Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced sanctions on the International Criminal Court as an institution, banning transactions with it after a six-month grace period, with exemptions for some telecoms, software, pension and detainee-related payments.
European states, Canada, Japan and the UN publicly backed the court. Reports of the plan had surfaced in September.
The court issued arrest warrants for Netanyahu and former defence minister Yoav Gallant in November 2024.

items.dek: The award came two weeks after the US sanctions; former ICC judge Navi Pillay also won the Nobel Peace Prize this month.
body: The European Parliament gave the 2026 Sakharov Prize for human rights to the International Criminal Court, less than two weeks after Washington's sanctions.
ICC President Tomoko Akane said the prize reaffirmed the importance of independent courts at a time of unprecedented challenges.

items.dek: Nicaragua argues German arms exports to Israel breach the Genocide Convention.
body: The International Court of Justice held hearings on Germany's preliminary objections in the case Nicaragua brought two years ago over German arms exports to Israel.
Germany said the case was improperly filed because Nicaragua did not seek to resolve the dispute first; Nicaragua pointed to correspondence with Berlin and asked the court to let the case proceed.

items.headline: Colombia withdraws its intervention in South Africa's genocide case
items.dek: The ICJ case file shows the withdrawal; the next written pleading, South Africa's Reply, is due in November 2027.
body: The ICJ's case page for South Africa v. Israel records that Colombia withdrew its Article 63 declaration of intervention on 22 September 2026. It had filed it in April 2024.

Israel filed its Counter-Memorial in March 2026, raising objections to jurisdiction. A 21 May 2026 order gives South Africa until 22 November 2027 for its Reply and Israel until 22 May 2029 for a Rejoinder.
The United States, Hungary, Fiji, Namibia, Iceland and the Netherlands were among states that filed declarations in March 2026.

items.dek: French, Belgian and Polish diplomats and a French mayor were targeted; the EU demanded accountability.
body: Masked settlers attacked a delegation of French, Belgian and Polish diplomats and Catholic Church representatives near Taybeh on 17 October, smashing a window of a Belgian diplomatic car.

Bernard Baudoux, the 78-year-old mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries, said he was thrown to the ground, kicked and beaten. The EU condemned the attack on 18 October; OCHA also recorded a consular vehicle damaged and a Palestinian man injured.

items.headline: Rome prosecutors put Israel Katz and 12 officials under investigation over flotilla detainees
items.dek: Fifty Italians detained from Gaza-bound boats in 2025 and 2026 alleged torture and other abuse.
body: Rome prosecutors widened a probe that had centred on Itamar Ben-Gvir to include Defence Minister Israel Katz, military chief Eyal Zamir and 11 other senior military, police and prison officials.
The case covers suspected torture, kidnapping, injury, robbery and damage during the interception of Global Sumud Flotilla boats, after complaints from 50 Italian citizens.

items.dek: The prisoner-rights group, outlawed by Israel in 2021, was searched along with a women's committees union.
body: Israeli forces searched the Ramallah offices of Addameer Prisoner Support and Human Rights Association and the Union of Palestinian Women's Committees, confiscating Addameer equipment, Al Jazeera's correspondent reported.

Snipers were also deployed at the entrances to the Palestine Medical Complex, the largest government hospital in the West Bank, according to Wafa. Addameer is among the groups Israel designated as terrorist organisations.

items.headline: Adalah documents a two-track discipline system for Palestinian students
items.dek: Proceedings were opened at about 40 institutions, mostly over social media posts.
body: Adalah's report on Palestinian students since 7 October 2023 says universities and colleges disciplined Palestinian students, mostly Israeli citizens, over private posts while ignoring extreme content from Jewish-Israeli students.

Adalah received 132 inquiries and represented or advised 100 students. In more than 80 cases students were suspended before any hearing, and in 20 cases they were expelled or suspended for one to five years.

items.dek: The network said the rhetoric endangers its journalists.
body: In his General Assembly speech, Netanyahu called Al Jazeera one of the world's "toxic media outlets" and accused it of turning young people against Israel.
Al Jazeera Media Network said it categorically rejected the remarks, describing them as part of a sustained campaign against the network and a risk to its staff.

items.dek: Brad Lander was released with a warning; dozens of rabbis and international volunteers remained in custody.
body: Israeli soldiers and police detained roughly 80 volunteers helping Palestinian farmers pick olives near Nahalin, according to Rabbis for Human Rights. They included American, Israeli, Palestinian, British and Canadian volunteers.
Brad Lander, the Democratic nominee and former New York City comptroller, said he was freed with a warning because of his profile and called for the others to be released.

items.headline: Police arrest a 94-year-old human rights barrister for backing Palestine Action
items.dek: Margaret Owen had spent months displaying signs supporting the proscribed group.
body: Margaret Owen OBE, a 94-year-old Jewish human rights barrister, was finally arrested at the end of September for showing support for Palestine Action, which the UK proscribed under the Terrorism Act in July 2025.

She told Al Jazeera she had attended about a dozen protests with a sign reading that she opposed genocide and supported the group, and had even written to the police confessing. Thousands have been detained in the UK for similar signs.

items.headline: Filton activists appeal first UK ruling to treat property damage as terrorism
items.dek: Four people were convicted of criminal damage "with a terrorist connection" over a 2024 raid on an Israeli arms maker.
body: Charlotte Head, Samuel Corner, Leona Kamio and Fatema Zainab Rajwani are appealing their convictions over the August 2024 raid on an Israeli arms factory in Filton near Bristol.
Supporters say it is the first time a British court has classed property damage as terrorism, and warn it could be used against other protests over violations of international law.

timeline.event: Return attempt under court decision; settlers torch two homes overnight
OCHA records the attack and the blocked return

cases.title: Petition against the Death Penalty for Terrorists Law (HCJ 76304-03-26)
cases.summary: Rights groups and Palestinian MKs asked the Supreme Court to void the March 2026 law, which in military courts makes death the near-default sentence for West Bank Palestinians. The State was ordered to respond by 24 May 2026; by October the government was weighing its first use.

timeline.event: Knesset passes the law 62-48; petition filed that night
Court orders State response by 24 May
Cabinet examines applying the law to the Neveh Tzuf suspect

sources.title: Urgent petition to Israeli Supreme Court against the Death Penalty Law
Ben Gvir pushes death penalty after Neveh Tzuf attack

sources.outlet: Public Committee Against Torture in Israel
sources.title: First case in which racist new Death Penalty Law could be applied

points.text: In the West Bank it rests on sections 284-294 of Military Order 1651 (the consolidated Security Provisions Order). A commander can order detention if there are reasonable grounds to think security requires it.
Each order lasts up to six months and can be renewed again and again with no maximum, so people can be held for years without trial.

A military judge must approve the order within eight days, but most of the material is withheld from the detainee and lawyer. Appeals go to the military appeals court and then the High Court, which rarely intervenes.
In June 2026 the Supreme Court upheld the continued detention of Dr Hussam Abu Safiya on confidential material his lawyers never saw.
Israel held 3,101 administrative detainees in October 2026, against 1,264 in September 2023 and a peak of 3,661 in April 2024.
An internal army document reported by Haaretz showed a 99.74% conviction rate in military courts in 2010: 25 acquittals in 9,542 cases.

West Bank Palestinians are tried in Israeli military courts such as the one at Ofer; the 2026 death-penalty amendments to West Bank military orders apply only to Palestinians, the petitioners against the law point out.

Since March 2026 military courts must impose death in most deadly-attack convictions of West Bank residents, can do so by simple majority even if prosecutors do not ask, and the commander can no longer commute.
A separate 2026 law created a special military tribunal for people accused over 7 October 2023, also empowered to impose death.
The Incarceration of Unlawful Combatants Law (2002) allows prolonged detention without trial with fewer safeguards than administrative detention. Most Gaza detainees are held under it.
Wartime amendments allow a person to be held 33 days before seeing a judge and 21 days before meeting a lawyer.
The Israel Prison Service held 1,419 people under the law in October 2026. The figure peaked at 2,673 in October 2025 before the prisoner releases.
Israel stopped informing the ICRC about Palestinian detainees after 7 October 2023. The High Court ordered cooperation to resume on 3 June 2026; HaMoked says the ruling has not yet been implemented.
In a third of HaMoked's 5,991 tracing requests for Gaza residents, the army said it had no indication of the person. 38 people in HaMoked's habeas cases were never found.

At the end of 2025, 351 Palestinian children were in Israel Prison Service custody and 51% of them were administrative detainees, the highest number and share since 2008. Children in army interrogation centres are not counted.
Palestinian prisoner institutions counted more than 350 children held in September 2026, in Megiddo and Ofer prisons.
More than 2,000 children have been detained since October 2023, according to the Palestinian Prisoner's Society.
Walid Ahmad, 17, died in Megiddo in March 2025; a judge stopped the inquiry despite evidence of starvation.
Defense for Children International-Palestine, the main source of child-detention data, closed on 7 April 2026 after years of Israeli pressure.
At the UN Human Rights Council in June 2026, Defence for Children International said at least 350 children were in IPS custody, many held on secret files and renewed at the last minute.

The Civil Administration told the Knesset in 2023 that it rejects 95% of Palestinian building applications in Area C and grants fewer than 10 permits a year; Bimkom's data for 2016-2020 shows 24 approvals out of 2,550.
More than 1,700 people were displaced by permit demolitions in 2025, the highest annual total on record.
About 1,790 people were displaced by permit-related demolitions in the West Bank from January to 19 October 2026, 668 of them in East Jerusalem.
The demolition of a five-storey building in At Tur on 6 October 2026 displaced 69 people, the largest single East Jerusalem displacement since 2009.
Since January 2023, 133 communities have been displaced by settler attacks and access restrictions; 49 were emptied entirely, 13 of them in 2026.
South Africa filed its genocide case against Israel on 29 December 2023. The ICJ ordered provisional measures on 26 January 2024, then added and modified them on 28 March and 24 May 2024.
Israel filed its Counter-Memorial in March 2026 with objections to jurisdiction. South Africa's Reply is due 22 November 2027 and Israel's Rejoinder 22 May 2029.

On 19 July 2024 the ICJ advised that Israel's continued presence in the occupied territory is unlawful, must end as rapidly as possible, and that settlement activity must stop and settlers be evacuated, with reparation owed.

On 22 October 2025 the ICJ advised that Israel, as occupying power, must ensure food, water and medical care reach civilians, facilitate UN relief including UNRWA, and must not use starvation as a method of warfare.

On 21 November 2024 ICC judges issued arrest warrants for Benjamin Netanyahu and Yoav Gallant for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity from at least 8 October 2023 to at least 20 May 2024, and for Hamas commander Mohammed Deif.
In October 2026 the US imposed sanctions on the ICC as an institution; the European Parliament then awarded the court the Sakharov Prize.

orgs.name: Addameer Prisoner Support and Human Rights Association
orgs.description: Palestinian group supporting political prisoners held by Israel, giving legal aid and publishing prisoner counts.

orgs.name: Al-Haq
orgs.description: Ramallah-based Palestinian human rights organisation documenting violations since 1979.

orgs.name: HaMoked: Center for the Defence of the Individual
orgs.description: Israeli group giving free legal aid to Palestinians on detention, residency, movement and demolitions; publishes monthly IPS detention figures.

orgs.name: B'Tselem
orgs.description: Israeli Information Center for Human Rights in the Occupied Territories, known for field documentation and detention statistics.

orgs.name: Defense for Children International-Palestine (closed)
orgs.description: Documented arrests and military prosecutions of Palestinian children until it ceased operations on 7 April 2026; its old domain no longer belongs to it.

orgs.name: Adalah - The Legal Center for Arab Minority Rights in Israel
orgs.description: Legal centre litigating for Palestinian citizens of Israel and residents of the occupied territory in Israeli courts.

orgs.name: Public Committee Against Torture in Israel (PCATI)
orgs.description: Israeli group that litigates and documents torture and ill-treatment, and campaigns against the death penalty.

orgs.name: Al Mezan Center for Human Rights
orgs.description: Independent Gaza-based human rights organisation; represents Gaza detainees including Dr Hussam Abu Safiya.

orgs.name: Palestinian Centre for Human Rights (PCHR)
orgs.description: Gaza-founded rights group publishing field documentation, including West Bank demolitions.

orgs.name: Yesh Din - Volunteers for Human Rights
orgs.description: Israeli group monitoring settler violence and law enforcement in the West Bank.

orgs.name: Physicians for Human Rights Israel (PHRI)
orgs.description: Israeli medical rights group that visits and advocates for detainees, including detained Gaza doctors.

orgs.name: Bimkom - Planning and Human Rights
orgs.description: Planners and architects working on planning rights for communities under Israeli control, including Area C and East Jerusalem.

orgs.name: Ir Amim
orgs.description: Israeli organisation focused on Jerusalem, tracking evictions, settlement and planning in the city.

orgs.name: Society of St Yves - Catholic Center for Human Rights
orgs.description: Legal aid centre in Jerusalem working for the dignity of all in the Holy Land, including residency and demolition cases.

orgs.name: Association for Civil Rights in Israel (ACRI)
orgs.description: Israel's oldest civil rights group; petitioned against the 2026 death penalty law.
